One sentence. Pick up the red cube, and hold it five centimetres above the table. No demonstrations. No training data.
First try: eight robots, eight failures. Every lift stopped at four point nine three centimetres. Less than a millimetre short.
So it read its own failures, rewrote its code, and tried again. Eight out of eight.
Then fifty layouts it had never seen. Fifty out of fifty. Total cost: under one cent.
This is Knack. Robots that learn by practising.
Teaching a robot arm a new task today takes days of hand-written code, or a hundred human demonstrations. Most labs, classrooms and makers have neither. Knack lets the robot practise instead.

Here's who does what. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super, on Nebius Token Factory, writes the robot's program. Eight simulated arms run it in parallel on random layouts, seeing only through OpenCV. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning reads every failed trace and names the lines that broke. Super rewrites, keeps what worked, and rolls back if it gets worse. The result is plain Python. No model in the control loop.

This is the live console, on a fresh run, sped up. Every tile is a real physics episode. The header counts tokens and dollars per model, live. When a round fails, the trace model explains why, and you can read the exact diff. Round by round, the robots turn green. Then the skill is tested on layouts it never practised on, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval, and a receipt.

Two findings. First, practice pays off most when perception is noisy. With camera-grade noise, Super went from six percent to eighty-two percent on a pushing task, just by practising. Second, a vision-language judge approved lifts that stopped a millimetre short. A skill trained against it scored zero out of fifty on ground truth. So Knack measures. It doesn't trust.

Every model call runs on Nebius Token Factory, so a skill costs cents, and every number here is in the open-source repo. Next: the same skill API on a real low-cost arm. Knack. Practice, not demonstrations.
